Introductions

Please briefly introduce yourself:

  • Your name and current role
  • One sentence on your connection/experience with AI in education


This session operates under the Chatham House rule.

Participants are free to use the information discussed during the session, but the identity and affiliation of any speaker (and their individual judgements) may not be revealed outside this room without their explicit consent.

In the session record, individual responses will be identified by letter code only. No names or institutional affiliations will be attached to specific numbers or opinions in any publication or report.

What we are doing today

This session is part of a study on the factors that drive or prevent the adoption of AI tutors in schools.


  • Expert judgement is a central source of evidence when published data are sparse or contested
  • Structured elicitation converts your knowledge into a form that is documented, reproducible and combinable with other evidence
  • We follow the Sheffield Elicitation Framework (SHELF), a well-established protocol for exactly this kind of exercise


There are no right or wrong answers. We are asking you to represent your genuine state of knowledge as accurately as you can.

A practice question

Before we work on the main question, we will practise with a quantity so that you can get comfortable with the format.


Training quantity

What percentage of Australian adults currently use ChatGPT or a similar AI chatbot (e.g. Gemini, Copilot, Claude) on a weekly basis?


We will go through a five-step process: plausible range, median, tertiles. Write your answers on the sheet provided. We will compare answers at the end.

Training: lower plausible limit L

Your lower plausible limit L is the percentage such that you judge it extremely unlikely that the true weekly usage rate is lower than L.

  • Think about what you know about digital technology use in Australia
  • Consider that ChatGPT launched publicly in late 2022; widespread awareness has grown significantly since then
  • L = 0% is always valid if you think very low usage is plausible, but is it actually plausible that fewer than L% use these tools weekly?


Challenge: If you later heard that the true figure was below your L, would you suspect the survey was flawed or would you accept it as plausible? Your reaction should be the former.


Write down your L now.

Training: upper plausible limit U

Your upper plausible limit U is the percentage such that you judge it extremely unlikely that the true weekly usage rate is higher than U.

  • Consider barriers: not everyone has internet access, a smartphone, or awareness of these tools
  • Consider that “weekly” is a relatively high bar for regular use
  • How high could weekly usage plausibly be, given what you know?


Check: You should now be almost certain that the true percentage lies between your L and your U.


Write down your U now.

Training: median M

Your median M is the percentage such that you judge it equally likely that the true weekly usage rate is below M or above M.

  • Do not simply split the difference between L and U
  • Is the distribution of your beliefs symmetric around some central value, or skewed towards the lower or upper end of your plausible range?


Challenge: Imagine a prize for correctly guessing whether the true value is above or below your M. You should have no preference for guessing either way.


Write down your M now.

Training: tertiles T1 and T2

Your lower tertile T1 and upper tertile T2 divide the plausible range into three equally probable regions.

T1 lies between L and M; T2 lies between M and U.


Reminder: Values near L and U are barely plausible; values near M are most plausible. So the central third (T1 to T2) of the probability mass occupies a narrower slice of the numerical range than the outer thirds.


Write down your T1 and T2 now.

Training: comparing answers

Discussion:

  1. How wide is the spread of medians across the group? What does that tell us about the state of shared knowledge on this topic?

  2. Are there participants whose plausible ranges do not overlap? What evidence or reasoning might explain that gap?

  3. How do your individual estimates compare with the reference data on the next slide? What does the comparison tell you about potential biases (towards optimism, pessimism, or anchoring on memorable figures)?


This exercise is purely for calibration. There is no penalty for being far off; the goal is to surface the reasoning behind your judgements before we apply the same process to our main question.

Training: reference data

GWI consumer survey, Australia, 2025

Approximately 25–30% of Australian internet users reported using an AI chatbot (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Copilot) in the past month.


Two caveats when comparing this to your estimates:

  • The GWI figure is for monthly use, not weekly. Weekly active users will be a subset of this.
  • The figure covers internet users, not all Australian adults; non-users of the internet are excluded.

The weekly figure is not directly measured in major public surveys. If you estimated 15–25% for weekly use, that is consistent with this evidence.

What we are trying to quantify

Focal question

What percentage of schools will have adopted AI tutors within the next five years?


This question serves as an anchor for today’s discussion.

Defining “AI tutor”

An AI tutor is a software system that interacts directly with an individual student (through conversation, adaptive exercises, or both) to support their learning in one or more school subjects. It adjusts its responses or content based on the student’s inputs, and is intended to supplement, not replace, the role of a classroom teacher.

In this study, we focus on AI tutors used by school students as part of their schooling, whether in the classroom or at home.

Defining “adopted”

For the purposes of today’s exercise, a school has adopted an AI tutor if:

  • At least one AI tutor product is in active, regular use by students at that school as part of their schooling
  • The use is sanctioned by the school (i.e., not purely independent student use)
  • The tool is used at least once per week on average during the school year

Scope: which schools?

For today’s exercise, we use Australian K–12 schools as the reference population, covering government, Catholic and independent sectors.

The five-year horizon runs from the start of 2026 to the end of 2030.


Approximate baseline context:

  • ~10,000 K–12 schools in Australia
  • AI tutor products are currently available and in limited use
  • No large-scale national adoption programme currently exists

Experience

Before we begin, we ask each participant to briefly declare any interests that could be perceived as influencing your judgements today.

This may include:

  • Current or recent employment or consultancy with AI technology companies
  • Financial interests in AI education products or related ventures
  • Advocacy roles for or against AI in education
  • Research grants or funding from parties with a stake in this question

Declarations are noted in the session record. They do not disqualify you from participating (they help us interpret the elicited judgements appropriately).

Expertise in the room

Please briefly describe the aspect of your expertise that is most directly relevant to today’s question. For example:

  • First-hand experience of AI tools in school settings
  • Research on technology adoption in education
  • Policy experience at school, system or government level
  • Knowledge of the AI tutor product landscape
  • Understanding of teacher or student behaviour

What expertise might be missing?

Consider the question: “What percentage of schools will have adopted AI tutors within the next five years?”

Are there perspectives or knowledge domains that are not represented in today’s group that could meaningfully shift the answer?

Key evidence: what do you know?

Before we move to the quantitative elicitation, we would like to hear from you:

  • What are the key sources of evidence you would draw on to answer the focal question?
  • Are there data, studies, or reports you consider particularly credible or informative?
  • Are there bodies of evidence you think are weak?

Probability elicitation

We use the tertile method from SHELF. You will be asked to provide five numbers:


Number Meaning
L Lower plausible limit
U Upper plausible limit
M Median
T1 Lower tertile
T2 Upper tertile


Each judgement is made privately and independently before any group discussion.

Step 1: Lower plausible limit L

Your lower plausible limit L is the value such that you judge it extremely unlikely that the true percentage of schools adopting AI tutors within five years could be less than L.

  • Not physically impossible, just extremely unlikely
  • If you think the true value could be very close to zero, you may use 0% as your L


Challenge: Imagine someone later tells you the true percentage turned out to be less than your L. Your reaction should be to strongly suspect their data or method, not to accept it as plausible.


Write down your L now.

Step 2: Upper plausible limit U

Your upper plausible limit U is the value such that you judge it extremely unlikely that the true percentage could be more than U.

  • Not physically impossible, just extremely unlikely
  • If you think near-universal adoption is plausible within five years, your U may be close to 100%


Check: You are now almost certain that the true percentage lies between your L and your U. Any value outside this range is, in your judgement, not plausible.


Write down your U now.

Step 3: Median M

Your median M is the value such that you judge it equally likely that the true percentage is below M or above M.

  • M must lie between your L and U
  • Do not simply split the difference between L and U. Think carefully about whether the true value is more likely to be closer to L or to U, and by how much


Challenge: Imagine a large prize for correctly guessing whether the true percentage is above or below your M, with no penalty for being wrong. You should have no preference for guessing either way.


Write down your M now.

Step 4: Tertiles T1 and T2

Your lower tertile T1 and upper tertile T2 divide the plausible range into three regions of equal probability.

It follows that T1 lies between L and M, and T2 lies between M and U.


Note: The interval from T1 to T2 will generally be narrower than the tails from L to T1 or from T2 to U, because values near the plausible limits are barely plausible whereas values near M are very plausible.


Write down your T1 and T2 now.

Checking your five numbers

You should now have: L, T1, M, T2, U


Check the following before you finalise your judgements:

  1. Order: L < T1 < M < T2 < U: are your numbers in this order?

  2. Spread of tails: The gaps L to T1 and T2 to U should each be wider than the gap T1 to T2: does that hold?

  3. Median check: If offered a prize for guessing whether the true value is above or below M, do you still have no preference?

  4. Tertile check: Do you believe the true value is equally likely to be below T1, between T1 and T2, or above T2?

Discussing the fitted distributions


Discussion prompts:

  1. What is the range of opinion across the group? Are there clear clusters or outliers?

  2. For experts whose M is notably higher or lower than others: what is the key piece of evidence or reasoning that underlies your position?

  3. Is there a piece of evidence or argument that, if it turned out to be true, would substantially shift your median upward? Downward?

What drives the differences?

The differences between individual distributions often reveal the factors that matter most.

Consider:

  1. Are the differences mainly about how fast adoption could happen, or about whether it will reach high levels at all?

  2. Are there particular barriers (cost, trust, teacher workload, curriculum fit) or enablers (policy mandates, product quality, parent demand) that different experts are weighting differently?

  3. Is there new evidence that, if gathered, would most reduce the uncertainty in the room?

Identifying the factors

We now move from the quantitative question to the qualitative drivers behind it.


Over the next session we will:

  1. Define the driving factors that influence AI tutor adoption in schools
  2. Rank those factors according to their perceived level of influence


The comparison attribute for ranking is:

“Level of influence on the adoption of AI tutors in individual classrooms”

Generating a factor list

Consider:

  • Factors at the school level
  • Factors at the teacher level
  • Factors at the student or parent level
  • Factors at the system level
  • Factors related to the technology itself

Consolidating the factor list


For each factor on the consolidated list, we need:

  • A short label (2–5 words)
  • A working definition (2–3 sentences) that is clear enough for two people to independently decide whether a given situation represents “more” or “less” of that factor


A factor is only useful for ranking if it is well-defined. Take time now to resolve any ambiguity. Vague factors produce unreliable rankings.

Factor definitions

For each factor, the definition should specify:


Element Example
What the factor is “Availability of technical support”
What “more” of it looks like “School has a dedicated IT coordinator and reliable helpdesk”
What “less” of it looks like “Teachers are solely responsible for troubleshooting AI tools”
Scope School-level factor; does not include external vendor support

Preliminary ranking exercise

Before the formal pairwise comparisons, we will do a quick individual ranking of the factors by level of influence on AI adoption in individual classrooms.


How we do this depends on how many factors we have:

  • Fewer factors: write them in rank order from most to least influential, working individually.
  • More factors: sort them into broad groups (e.g. high / medium / low influence), then order within groups as best you can.

Pairwise ranking

A simple rank order (1st, 2nd, 3rd, …) tells us nothing about how much more important the top-ranked factor is than the second, or how confident we are in any given ordering decision.


The Thurstone pairwise method addresses this by asking a different question for each pair of factors:

The pairwise comparison question

“Out of 100 classrooms deciding whether to adopt an AI tutor, in how many would [Factor A] be a stronger driver of that decision than [Factor B]? Give a number between 0 and 100, where 50 means the two factors are equally influential on average.”


These proportions are fitted to a statistical model (Thurstone, 1927) that places each factor on a continuous importance scale (and quantifies the uncertainty in that placement).

The comparison attribute

For all pairwise comparisons today, recall that the attribute is:


“Level of influence on the adoption of AI tutors in individual classrooms”

A factor has higher influence if, across a wide range of school contexts, its presence or absence is more likely to tip a classroom towards or away from adopting an AI tutor.


We are comparing factors on influence on adoption, not on their importance to student outcomes or to education policy more broadly. Keep this distinction in mind when making each comparison.

Individual pairwise comparisons

For each pair, write a number between 0 and 100:

  • 0: Factor A would never be a stronger driver than Factor B
  • 50: the two factors are equally influential on average
  • 100: Factor A would always be a stronger driver than Factor B

Comparing individual scales

Discussion prompts:

  1. Which factors appear near the top of most experts’ scales? Which are near the bottom? Are there any surprises?

  2. Which factors show large disagreement across experts (appearing high on some scales and low on others)? What reasoning might explain those differences?

  3. Are there any pairs of factors that you expect to be collinear (where knowing the value of one factor tells you a lot about the other)? If so, should they be treated as a single combined factor?

Tier boundaries and partition prior

The next step is to ask: are there natural groupings (clusters of factors that sit at a similar level of causal primacy in the adoption process)?


These groupings are the tiers of a root partition: a way of organising factors into layers based on how upstream or downstream they are in the causal story of AI adoption.

Tier boundaries and partition prior

Tier 1: background conditions. Factors that are largely set before any individual adoption decision is made; they shape the environment in which everything else operates.

Tier 2: intermediate factors. Things that vary across schools or classrooms given the background conditions.

Tier 3: proximate triggers. The immediate drivers of a specific adoption decision.


We are not asking whether a factor is important. We are asking whether it is upstream (a background condition that shapes the context) or downstream (a proximate cause that operates given the background).

Borderline factors

Not every factor will sit clearly in one tier. A factor is borderline if its scale value sits close to a proposed tier boundary (meaning the ranking does not confidently assign it to one tier rather than the adjacent one).


Borderline factors are not a problem: they are information. They tell us that the data will need to discriminate between two plausible tier assignments, which is precisely what the downstream analysis is designed to do.


For each proposed boundary, factors that fall within the uncertainty band will be treated as borderline. Both their possible tier assignments will be carried forward.

The viable partition set

Consider the central tier assignment (the partition that places each factor in the tier to which it was most confidently assigned).

  1. Does this grouping make substantive sense to you? Are there any factors whose tier assignment feels clearly wrong?

  2. For the borderline factors: which tier assignment do you think is more likely for each one, or do both assignments seem equally plausible?

  3. As a group: do we prefer a uniform prior over the viable partitions (treat all plausible tier assignments as equally likely), or should the central partition receive more prior weight (reflecting high confidence in the ranking)?

What this produces

The tier boundaries and borderline-factor judgements together define a prior distribution over root partitions: a probability distribution over the plausible ways of organising the factors into causal tiers.


Output Description
Tier assignment Each non-borderline factor placed in a single tier
Viable partitions All combinations of borderline-factor tier assignments
Prior weights Uniform or confidence-weighted across viable partitions
\(\phi_i(\ell)\) values Marginal probability that factor \(i\) belongs to tier \(\ell\)
